lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
Hard rock mining is the process of extracting gold from solid rock, rather than from loose soil or river gravel. In many parts of Africa, gold is locked inside quartz veins or sulphide-rich rock. This type of mining is more difficult and expensive than alluvial mining, but it can be very rewarding because the gold is often concentrated in specific veins. For example, a rich quartz vein can contain 5 to 30 grams of gold per tonne of rock, while alluvial gravel might only have 0.1 to 0.5 grams per cubic metre. Hard rock mining allows you to target these high-grade zones.

Why does it matter for African artisans? Many easy alluvial deposits are becoming exhausted. As surface gravels run out, miners must follow the gold into the bedrock. Hard rock mining also creates more stable, long-term jobs. A well-run hard rock operation can support a team of 10 to 20 people for years, rather than a few months. In countries like Tanzania, Ghana, South Africa, and Zimbabwe, small-scale hard rock mining is a major source of income for rural communities.

However, hard rock mining requires different skills. You need to break rock, support underground tunnels, ventilate the workings, and process the ore. It is dangerous if done carelessly. This module will teach you the basics: which tools to use, how to drill and blast, how to avoid common mistakes, and how to stay safe. You will also learn a practical exercise to test your understanding.

By the end of this module, you will be able to identify a gold-bearing vein, set up a small hard rock mine, extract ore efficiently, and process it to recover gold. Remember: hard rock mining is a team effort. Always work with at least one other person, and never take shortcuts with safety. The gold is not worth your life.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To mine hard rock, you need the right tools. The basic kit includes: a heavy-duty pickaxe (2-3 kg head), a sledgehammer (4-6 kg), steel wedges (at least 3, 20-30 cm long), a crowbar (1.5 m), and a shovel. For drilling, you need a hand drill (also called a jumper) â a 1.5-2 m steel rod with a hardened, chisel-shaped bit. You will also need a striker (a smaller hammer to hit the drill) and a scraper (a spoon-shaped rod to clean the hole). If you can afford it, a petrol-powered rock drill (like a Cobra or Pionjar) will speed up work by 10 times, but many artisans start with hand tools.

For blasting, you need explosives. In most African countries, you must buy explosives legally from a licensed dealer. Common types are ammonium nitrate/fuel oil (ANFO) or dynamite. You will also need safety fuse, detonators (blasting caps), and a crimper. Never make homemade explosives â they are illegal and extremely dangerous. If you cannot access legal explosives, you can use non-explosive methods like expansive grout (e.g., Dexpan) or heating rock with fire and then quenching with water to crack it.

For support, you need timber poles (10-15 cm diameter) or steel arches, and wooden planks for lagging. For ventilation, a hand-cranked fan or a flexible duct with a small blower helps. For lighting, use rechargeable headlamps (at least 100 lumens) â never use open flames underground because of gas risk.

For processing ore, you need a hammer mill or stamp mill to crush rock, a sluice box or pan for concentration, and mercury or borax for amalgamation. Mercury is toxic â use it only with gloves and in a ventilated area. Borax is safer for small-scale smelting. Also get a sieve (0.5 mm) and a gold pan. Always wear PPE: hard hat, steel-toe boots, safety glasses, gloves, and dust mask. In Africa, many supplies are available in mining towns like Geita (Tanzania), Obuasi (Ghana), or Kadoma (Zimbabwe).

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Step 1: Find the vein. Look for quartz outcrops, especially those with iron staining (reddish-brown) or visible gold. Follow the vein by digging trenches along the surface. Once you find a promising spot, clear the area and mark a tunnel entrance about 1.5 m wide and 1.8 m high.

Step 2: Drill and blast. Using a hand drill, make holes 30-60 cm deep at a slight angle. For a typical round, drill 6 to 10 holes: one central cut hole, four corner holes, and two lifters (bottom holes). Clean each hole with a scraper. Insert a primer (detonator with a stick of dynamite) and fill the rest with ANFO. Tamp it gently with clay. Connect the safety fuse â make it long enough to give you at least 2 minutes to escape. Light the fuse and retreat to a safe distance (at least 50 m). Wait 30 minutes before returning.

Step 3: Remove broken rock. After blasting, wait for smoke and dust to clear. Use a crowbar to check for loose rocks on the roof and walls â scale them down. Then shovel the broken ore into wheelbarrows or buckets and transport it to the surface. Sort the ore: keep quartz and sulphide-rich pieces, discard waste rock.

Step 4: Support the tunnel. After each blast, install timber supports every 1-1.5 m. Use 10-15 cm diameter poles as posts and caps, and planks as lagging. If the ground is very loose, use steel arches or rock bolts. Never leave unsupported ground more than 2 m from the face.

Step 5: Ventilate and drain. Use a hand fan or flexible duct to push fresh air to the face. If water collects, dig a drainage ditch along one side and pump it out with a hand pump or bucket.

Step 6: Process the ore. Crush the ore to sand size (less than 2 mm) using a hammer mill or stamp mill. Then concentrate the gold using a sluice box or pan. For fine gold, use mercury amalgamation or borax smelting. Finally, melt the gold into a button or bar. Record your recovery â a good day's work might yield 1-5 grams from 100 kg of ore.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Mistake 1: Not supporting the roof. Many accidents happen because miners dig too far without timber. Fix: Install supports every 1-1.5 m. If you see cracks or hear popping sounds, get out and support immediately.

Mistake 2: Using too much explosive. Overcharging shatters the rock into dust and damages the tunnel. Fix: Use the right amount â typically 0.5-1 kg of ANFO per cubic metre of rock. Start with less and adjust.

Mistake 3: Poor ventilation. Underground air can become low in oxygen or filled with blasting fumes. Fix: Always ventilate for at least 30 minutes after blasting. Use a fan or duct. Never enter if you feel dizzy.

Mistake 4: Ignoring water. Water can flood your tunnel and weaken walls. Fix: Dig a drainage ditch and keep a hand pump. If water is heavy, drill a drainage hole ahead of the face.

Mistake 5: Losing gold in processing. Many miners crush ore too coarse, so gold remains locked in rock. Fix: Crush to less than 2 mm. Also, use a correct sluice angle (about 10-15 degrees) and proper water flow. Check tailings for gold â if you see any, re-run them.

Mistake 6: Using mercury without safety. Mercury is highly toxic. Fix: Use gloves, work outdoors, and never heat mercury indoors. Better: use borax smelting instead.

Mistake 7: Working alone. Hard rock mining is dangerous. Fix: Always work with at least one partner. Have someone outside who knows your plan and can call for help.

Mistake 8: Not testing the ore. Some miners dig for months without checking grade. Fix: Take a 5 kg sample every 2 m of tunnel and pan it. If you get less than 0.5 g per tonne, move to a new spot. This saves time and money.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Safety in hard rock mining is not optional. Follow these rules to stay alive. First, never enter an unsupported tunnel. Before starting work, check the roof and walls for loose rock. Use a crowbar to scale down any loose pieces. If you hear cracking or popping, evacuate immediately.

Second, always wear personal protective equipment (PPE): hard hat, steel-toe boots, safety glasses, gloves, dust mask, and headlamp. In dusty conditions, wear a respirator. Hearing protection is needed when using rock drills.

Third, handle explosives legally and carefully. Store explosives in a locked, dry box away from living areas. Never smoke or use open flames near explosives. Use only safety fuse and detonators â never improvise. After blasting, wait at least 30 minutes for fumes to clear before returning.

Fourth, ventilate. Underground air can contain carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, and silica dust. Use a hand-cranked fan or flexible duct to push fresh air to the face. If you feel dizzy, headache, or short of breath, get to the surface immediately.

Fifth, manage water. Flooding can trap you. Always have a drainage ditch and a hand pump. If water is rising fast, abandon the tunnel.

Sixth, work in teams. Never work alone underground. Have a buddy system, and tell someone on the surface where you are going and when you will return. Use a rope or communication system.

Seventh, practice good hygiene. Wash hands before eating. Mercury and lead dust can be absorbed. Do not eat or smoke underground.

Eighth, have an emergency plan. Know the nearest clinic or hospital. Keep a first aid kit with bandages, antiseptic, and painkillers. For serious injuries, have a stretcher and a way to call for help.

Best practice also includes regular training. Attend safety workshops offered by organizations like the Artisanal Gold Council or local mining departments. Keep your tunnel clean and organized. Store tools safely. And remember: no gold is worth your life. If a tunnel feels unsafe, leave it.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
This exercise will help you practice the key skills of hard rock mining. You will need: a hand drill, sledgehammer, wedges, a pickaxe, a shovel, a bucket, a gold pan, and a safe outdoor area with a rock outcrop (or a concrete block to simulate rock). Work with a partner.

Exercise 1: Drill a hole. Mark a spot on the rock. Hold the drill at a 70-degree angle. Strike the drill with the sledgehammer, rotating it a quarter turn after each hit. Drill to 30 cm depth. This should take about 15-20 minutes in medium-hard rock. Measure the hole and check that it is straight.

Exercise 2: Break rock with wedges. If you cannot use explosives, drill three holes in a line, 15 cm apart. Insert steel wedges into each hole. Hit them evenly with the sledgehammer until the rock cracks. This simulates a blast. Collect the broken pieces.

Exercise 3: Support a tunnel. Using timber poles, build a support frame 1.5 m wide and 1.8 m high. Use two posts, one cap, and lagging planks. Test its strength by pushing on it â it should not wobble.

Exercise 4: Process ore. Crush a 5 kg sample of the broken rock to sand size using a hammer or stamp mill. Pan the crushed material in a bucket of water. Swirl gently, letting lighter material wash away. Look for gold â it will be at the bottom of the pan. Weigh any gold you find (use a jeweler's scale). Calculate grade in grams per tonne.

Exercise 5: Safety check. Before starting, inspect your area for loose rocks. Put on all PPE. Practice scaling down a loose rock with a crowbar. Then, simulate an emergency: shout 'fire' and evacuate to a safe distance within 30 seconds.

After the exercise, write a short report: what you did, how long it took, how much gold you recovered (if any), and what you would do differently. This will build your confidence and skill. Remember, practice makes perfect. Repeat this exercise until you can drill, break, support, and process efficiently.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Hard Rock Mining for Artisan Gold Miners

This practical reference consolidates the operational knowledge needed to run a small-scale hard rock gold operation in Africa profitably and safely. Hard rock mining â extracting gold from solid ore rather than alluvial gravels â demands more capital, more skill, and stricter discipline than surface panning. But it also offers higher returns per tonne when done correctly. This module gives you the tools, numbers, and field-tested methods to assess, extract, crush, and process hard rock ore with confidence.

Key Operational Data

Hard rock mining economics hinge on three variables: grade (grams per tonne), recovery rate, and throughput. The table below gives typical ranges observed across African artisanal hard rock operations. Use these as planning benchmarks, not guarantees â always assay your own ore.

Table 1: Typical Operating Parameters for African Artisanal Hard Rock Gold Mining
Parameter Low Typical High Notes
Ore grade (g/t Au)1.54â815+Reef width and mineralisation control grade
Recovery (gravity + CIL)55%75â85%92%Depends on liberation size and reagent control
Throughput (t/day)210â30100Single stamp mill to ball mill scale
Ore body width (m)0.20.5â1.55+Narrow-vein mining is most common
Shaft depth (m)1030â60120+Deeper shafts need formal support and ventilation
Water inflow (L/min)<510â30>100Pumping capacity must exceed inflow
Diesel / power cost (USD/t)815â2540Energy is often the largest cost line
All-in cost (USD/t)2540â70120Labour, energy, reagents, maintenance

Source: Compiled from the Intergovernmental Forum on Mining, IGF Guidance for Governments: Managing Artisanal and Small-Scale Mining (2017), and the World Bank Artisanal and Small-Scale Mining (ASM) Handbook (2020). Figures are indicative planning ranges, not site-specific guarantees.

Grade, Recovery and Revenue â What the Numbers Mean

Understanding the relationship between grade, recovery and revenue is the single most important business skill in hard rock mining. A miner who moves 20 tonnes of 3 g/t ore at 70% recovery recovers about 42 grams of gold. At a gold price of USD 1,900/oz (roughly USD 61/g), that is about USD 2,560 in gross revenue â before labour, energy, reagents, and transport. If the same miner processes 20 tonnes of 8 g/t ore at 85% recovery, the revenue jumps to about USD 8,300. Grade and recovery are not abstract â they are the difference between a marginal operation and a profitable one.

Table 2 shows a simple sensitivity analysis. Use it to test whether your planned operation can survive a drop in grade or recovery. If your margin disappears at 3 g/t and 65% recovery, your operation is fragile.

Table 2: Gross Revenue Sensitivity (USD per 20 tonnes processed, gold at USD 1,900/oz)
Grade (g/t) Recovery 60% Recovery 75% Recovery 85% Recovery 92%

Source: Author's calculation using gold price of USD 1,900/oz (USD 61.08/g) and 20 t processed. Gold price reference: World Gold Council, Gold Price Data (2024). Recovery ranges based on IGF (2017) ASM processing benchmarks.

â  SAFETY WARNING â GROUND COLLAPSE AND METHANE

Never enter an unsupported tunnel or shaft deeper than 5 metres without timber or steel sets. Hard rock does not mean stable rock. In many African hard rock belts, sheared and weathered zones collapse without warning. Additionally, underground workings can accumulate methane, carbon monoxide from blasting, and low-oxygen air. Always ventilate before entry, never use open flame for lighting, and never work alone underground. Illegal or unregulated pits are the leading cause of mining fatalities in African ASM â official estimates attribute hundreds of deaths annually to tunnel collapse in countries such as Zimbabwe, Tanzania, and Ghana.

Step-by-Step Practical Method

The following method is the field-standard sequence for a small hard rock operation. Each step assumes you have legal mineral rights or a registered claim.

  1. Geological assessment. Map the reef strike and dip. Collect grab samples every 2â3 metres along the reef and submit for assay. Do not mine blind.
  2. Site preparation. Clear the portal area, establish drainage, and set up a secure ore pad. Locate your tailings pond downslope and away from watercourses.
  3. Drilling and blasting. Drill holes at 0.8â1.2 m spacing, charge with permitted explosives, and blast at the end of shift. Never return to the face until fumes have cleared.
  4. Mucking and haulage. Load broken ore into wheelbarrows or cocopans and haul to surface. Sort waste rock from ore at the face to reduce transport costs.
  5. Crushing and milling. Reduce ore to <10 mm with a jaw crusher, then mill to 75â150 microns in a ball mill or stamp mill. Liberation size determines recovery.
  6. Gravity concentration. Run milled pulp over a sluice, shaking table, or centrifuge to capture free gold. This is the cheapest recovery step.
  7. Chemical recovery (CIL/CIP). For fine gold locked in sulphides, use a licensed carbon-in-leach or carbon-in-pulp circuit. This requires trained operators and environmental controls.
  8. Smelting and sale. Smelt dorÃ© bars or sell concentrate to a licensed buyer. Record every gram â traceability is now required by most formal buyers.

Common Mistakes and Fixes

Mistake 1: Mining without assay data. Fix: assay a minimum of 10 samples before committing to a face. A USD 20 assay can save USD 2,000 in wasted labour.

Mistake 2: Over-crushing or under-crushing. Fix: sieve your milled product weekly. If more than 20% is coarser than 150 microns, your recovery will suffer.

Mistake 3: Poor ventilation. Fix: install a forced-air fan and flexible ducting. Test air quality before every shift.

Mistake 4: No tailings management. Fix: build a lined or clay-sealed tailings pond. Untreated tailings contaminate groundwater and trigger regulatory shutdowns.

Mistake 5: Selling unprocessed ore. Fix: process on-site where possible. Selling raw ore transfers most of the value to the buyer.

Mistake 6: Ignoring mercury and cyanide rules. Fix: use licensed reagents only, and never burn amalgam in the open. Mercury vapour is a permanent health hazard.

Safety and Best Practice

Safety is not a cost â it is a licence to operate. Formal buyers, banks, and regulators increasingly require documented safety and environmental compliance. The following practices are non-negotiable:

  • Support every tunnel with timber, steel, or rock bolts. Inspect supports daily.
  • Ventilate all underground workings. Test for oxygen, CO, and methane before entry.
  • Use personal protective equipment: helmet, boots, gloves, eye protection, and dust mask.
  • Store explosives in a locked, licensed magazine. Never store detonators with explosives.
  • Manage water: pump shafts dry, and never discharge untreated process water into rivers.
  • Train every worker on emergency evacuation and first aid. Keep a stretcher and first-aid kit on site.
  • Keep records: daily production, assay results, safety incidents, and reagent use.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. â Mineral rights or claim registered and valid.
  2. â Geological map and assay data for the working face.
  3. â Shaft and tunnel supports inspected and logged today.
  4. â Ventilation running and air quality tested before entry.
  5. â PPE issued and worn by every worker on site.
  6. â Crushing and milling circuit calibrated to liberation size.
  7. â Tailings pond contained, labelled, and away from watercourses.
  8. â Daily production and safety records completed.

Practical Exercise

Exercise: Grade-to-Revenue Calculation. You have blasted 15 tonnes of ore from a 0.8 m wide quartz reef. Assay returns 5.2 g/t Au. Your ball mill recovers 78% of gold. Gold price is USD 1,900/oz.

  1. Calculate total grams of gold in the ore.
  2. Calculate recovered grams after 78% recovery.
  3. Convert recovered grams to troy ounces (1 oz = 31.1035 g).
  4. Calculate gross revenue in USD.
  5. If your all-in cost is USD 55/tonne, calculate your profit or loss.

Answer guide: 15 t Ã 5.2 g/t = 78 g Au. 78 Ã 0.78 = 60.84 g recovered. 60.84 Ã· 31.1035 = 1.956 oz. 1.956 Ã 1,900 = USD 3,716. Cost = 15 Ã 55 = USD 825. Profit = USD 2,891.

Further Reading

  • Intergovernmental Forum on Mining (IGF) â ASM Guidance and Reports â free guidance documents on managing artisanal and small-scale mining.
  • World Bank â Extractive Industries and ASM Resources â free handbooks and country reports.
  • UN Environment Programme â Mercury and ASM â free technical guidance on mercury-free gold processing.
  • World Gold Council â Responsible Gold Mining Principles â free standards and price data.
  • African Union â Africa Mining Vision â free policy framework for mineral-based development.

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills programme. All figures are indicative and must be verified against site-specific assay and cost data. Always comply with national mining, environmental, and safety regulations.

quiz.q: What is hard rock mining?
options: A) Mining gold from river gravel
B) Mining gold from solid rock
quiz.explanation: Hard rock mining extracts gold from solid rock, not loose deposits.

quiz.q: Which of these is a typical gold grade in a rich quartz vein?
quiz.explanation: Rich quartz veins often contain 5-30 g/t gold.

quiz.q: Why is hard rock mining becoming more important in Africa?
options: A) Alluvial deposits are becoming exhausted
B) It is easier than alluvial mining
quiz.explanation: As surface gravels run out, miners must follow gold into bedrock.

quiz.q: Which tool is used for drilling holes in hard rock by hand?
quiz.explanation: A hand drill, or jumper, is a steel rod used for manual drilling.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a scraper in hard rock mining?
quiz.explanation: A scraper removes cuttings from the drill hole.

quiz.q: Which explosive is commonly used in small-scale mining?
quiz.explanation: ANFO (ammonium nitrate/fuel oil) is common and relatively safe.

quiz.q: What is a safe alternative to explosives for breaking rock?
quiz.explanation: Expansive grout and fire-quenching are non-explosive methods.

quiz.q: What is the minimum depth for a drill hole in a typical round?
quiz.explanation: Holes are typically 30-60 cm deep for efficient blasting.

quiz.q: How many holes are usually drilled in a small blast round?
quiz.explanation: A typical round has 6-10 holes for good breakage.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after blasting?
quiz.explanation: Wait at least 30 minutes for fumes and dust to clear.

quiz.q: What is scaling?
options: B) Removing loose rocks from roof and walls
quiz.explanation: Scaling removes loose rock to prevent falls.

quiz.q: How often should you install timber supports?
quiz.explanation: Supports every 1-1.5 m keep the tunnel stable.

quiz.q: What is the correct angle for a sluice box?
quiz.explanation: A 10-15 degree angle allows proper gold capture.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake in processing ore?
quiz.explanation: Coarse crushing leaves gold locked in rock.

quiz.q: Why is mercury dangerous?
quiz.explanation: Mercury is highly toxic and can cause brain damage.

quiz.q: What is a safer alternative to mercury for gold recovery?
quiz.explanation: Borax smelting is safer for small-scale miners.

quiz.q: What should you do if you feel dizzy underground?
options: B) Get to the surface immediately
quiz.explanation: Dizziness can indicate lack of oxygen or gas exposure.

quiz.q: How often should you take an ore sample to test grade?
quiz.explanation: Sampling every 2 m helps track grade and avoid waste.

quiz.q: What is the minimum number of people for safe underground work?
quiz.explanation: Always work with at least one partner for safety.

quiz.q: What PPE is essential for hard rock mining?
quiz.explanation: All listed PPE are essential for safety.

quiz.q: What should you do before lighting a blast fuse?
options: B) Ensure escape route is clear
quiz.explanation: All safety checks are necessary before blasting.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of ventilation underground?
quiz.explanation: Ventilation removes gases and supplies fresh air.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of tunnel collapse?
quiz.explanation: Unsupported ground is the main cause of collapses.

quiz.q: How can you test a timber support's strength?
options: B) Hit it with a hammer
quiz.explanation: A gentle push checks for wobbling or weakness.

quiz.q: What is the recommended crush size for ore before panning?
quiz.explanation: Crushing to less than 2 mm liberates gold particles.

quiz.q: What is the first step in hard rock mining?
quiz.explanation: You must locate a gold-bearing vein before mining.

quiz.q: What does a reddish-brown stain on quartz indicate?
quiz.explanation: Iron staining often indicates gold-bearing quartz.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a drainage ditch in a tunnel?
quiz.explanation: Drainage ditches prevent flooding and weakening of walls.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find less than 0.5 g/t in your sample?
options: B) Move to a new spot
quiz.explanation: Low grade means the vein is not economic; move on.

quiz.q: What is the safest way to store explosives?
options: A) In a locked, dry box
quiz.explanation: Explosives must be stored securely and away from heat.
